passage: Dear Ramesh Sir, you asked why the class group was full of arguments on Monday. Partly, that was my fault. On Saturday night a forwarded message said students had been beaten at the candle march and hospitals were overflowing. It came with a photo, and I felt my chest burn. Within a minute I had sent it to four groups, thinking I was helping the cause. By Sunday afternoon a classmate whose brother was really at the march told us the message was old and from another city. Two friends had already posted furious comments. Now half the class thinks the organisers lied, and one girl refuses to sign our petition. I should have checked before pressing send. I am sorry. Yours, Vidya

qa.q: How many groups did Vidya forward the message to?
What was Vidya feeling when the message arrived?
qa.a: Anger and alarm: Vidya's chest burned and the urge to act at once made forwarding feel like helping.

qa.q: What could Vidya have done instead of forwarding straight away, and why?
qa.a: Vidya could have checked the photo and its date with a reliable source or asked a teacher first, because a quick check would have stopped a false claim spreading and protected the cause.

qa.q: How might Ramesh Sir see the class arguments?
qa.a: Ramesh Sir sees a class divided by a false message and wants to understand how it started, so Vidya's honest account helps Ramesh Sir deal with it.

grounding: A teen forwards dramatic unchecked messages as action, and the false message causes confusion and weakens the cause.

passage:
So, Sahil, you asked why I stopped forwarding stuff. Fine. Here's the story.

I'm Tejas. When the school announced the new uniform rule, everyone was angry. And then these messages started coming. "Principal took money from uniform shop!" "Students fined 5000 for wrong socks!" I was angry too, so I forwarded every one to three groups. It felt like I was doing something. Like fighting.

Then our class teacher showed us the actual circular. No fines. No shop deal. Just a rule about colours. The "5000 fine" message came from a joke page.

A lot of parents had already called the school, furious. The real complaint, that the new uniform was expensive, got lost under all the fake ones.

That was the worst part. I'd helped bury the one point that was true. Now I check before I forward. It's slower, but it's actually on our side.

qa.q: What did the actual circular say?
qa.a: No fines, no shop deal, just a rule about colours.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel on learning the messages were false?
qa.a: Tejas felt embarrassed and guilty, having helped bury the one true complaint.

qa.q: What else could Tejas do next time a dramatic message arrives?
qa.a: Tejas could check the school's official circular or ask a teacher first, and only forward what can be confirmed.

qa.q: How did the forwarded messages affect the parents who called the school?
qa.a: The parents were misled into calling about fake fines, so their energy went to the false claims instead of the real cost problem.

grounding: A spoken account of a teen who forwards dramatic unverified messages about an issue, spreading confusion and weakening the real complaint.

passage:
I'm Bhupen, and I'm in the same tuition batch as Farida. During the week of the college seat protest, I watched her phone buzz non-stop.

She'd read something, gasp, and forward it immediately. A video of "police beating students", a list of "arrested names", a voice note saying colleges would be shut for a month. She sent them to our batch group, her family group, the society group. She said, "People need to know!"

On Thursday our teacher looked at the video and quietly pointed out the signboards in it were in another language. It was from a different country, years ago. The list of names had a boy from our batch in it who was sitting right there.

Farida went red and put her phone face-down. For the rest of the class she didn't touch it.

I don't know exactly what she felt. But she didn't forward anything that evening.

qa.q: What did the teacher point out about the video?
qa.a: The signboards in it were in another language; it was from a different country, years ago.

qa.q: What might Farida have been feeling when she put her phone face-down?
qa.a: She probably felt ashamed and embarrassed, realising she had spread false posts to many groups.

qa.q: What could Farida do before forwarding the next dramatic message?
qa.a: She could check where it came from and whether a trusted source confirms it, and simply not forward it if she can't.

qa.q: How did Farida's forwarding look to Bhupen?
qa.a: To Bhupen it looked like quick, well-meant action that turned into spreading confusion, though Bhupen can't be sure what she felt.

grounding: An observer describes a teen forwarding dramatic unverified messages about a protest, which turn out false and spread confusion.
